title: Diamond-Complete: The Shape of Work That Compounds with AI
author: Anthea Roberts · Sue Brake

dom.t: Staffing structure: AI threatens both pyramid and pipeline

st.t: Staffing structure: AI threatens both pyramid and pipeline
st.an: The source accepts that AI reshapes professional work and materially extends the cluster’s expertise theme by specifying a competence model that combines domain depth, cross-disciplinary breadth and AI fluency. It explains why substantive expertise remains necessary to direct AI and verify its output, while addressing individual capabilities rather than providing evidence about firm staffing shapes or pipeline effects.
qs: But with no domain of their own, they can't tell when the AI is confidently wrong, and they compete with the model on exactly the ground where it's strongest.

kp.k: Expertise shapes frame AI augmentation and displacement
kp.d: Roberts and Brake propose a cross-domain conceptual framework in which depth and breadth of expertise predict whether AI enhances or erodes a person's value better than job title, industry or seniority. Their I, dash and T shapes describe individual capabilities, not organisational staffing structures. The argument is presented as the authors' interpretation rather than a measured empirical finding.
qs: The shape of a person's expertise — how deep it runs, how wide it reaches — predicts, better than almost anything else, whether AI compounds your value or erodes it.
The **I** is pure depth.
The **dash**, for want of a better letter, is pure breadth.
The **T** is both.

kp.k: Pre-AI expertise involved distinct strengths and vulnerabilities
kp.d: The authors characterise specialists as valuable through irreplaceable depth but vulnerable to narrowness and field changes; generalists as valuable for connecting silos but dependent on experts; and T-shaped professionals as combining trusted expertise with cross-team leadership. They argue that developing the latter historically required both years of practice and curiosity across disciplines.
qs: The I-shape's strength was irreplaceability.
Its weakness was brittleness.
With no real depth, there was always a point where you had to hand off to someone who actually knew.
Their only genuine weakness was that they were expensive and slow to grow.

kp.k: Rising AI capability progressively exposes narrow specialists
kp.d: The authors argue that specialists initially underestimated AI because they could still outperform it in their own domains. They describe capability advancing from school-level work through undergraduate and graduate work toward professional judgment, with routine expert tasks exposed first and genuine edge-case judgment lasting longest. Tax lawyers appear among their examples of narrow specialists; no profession-specific displacement measurements are supplied.
qs: AI capability has been climbing the ladder of expertise for years: competent first at school level, then undergraduate, then graduate, and now pressing into professional judgment itself.
The routine parts of expert work go first; the genuine edge-case judgment holds out longest.
The pure specialist, with only that one stroke to stand on, is more exposed than anyone expected.

kp.d: The authors contend that generalists initially experience AI as an amplifier of their ability to connect fields and synthesise unfamiliar subjects. Their proposed displacement mechanism is that AI makes those same capabilities abundant and inexpensive, eroding the premium for breadth without depth. This is an asserted market interpretation, not an evidenced estimate of employment or pricing effects.
qs: Generalists tend to *love* AI, because it does the very thing they prize: ranging across unfamiliar fields, connecting dots, pulling together a credible view of something they only half knew an hour ago.
The thing the generalist was paid a premium for is now abundant and nearly free.
The tool that felt like an amplifier turns out to be the substitute.

kp.k: AI direction becomes a separate professional capability
kp.d: The authors add an upward stroke representing the ability to brief, evaluate and correct AI, distinguishing it from knowing prompts. They state that this capability barely existed as a category three years earlier. Adding it alone does not resolve other weaknesses: AI-enabled specialists remain narrow, while AI-fluent generalists can catalyse adoption but lack the domain anchor needed to identify confident errors.
qs: The ability to direct, brief, evaluate, and correct AI well.
Not knowing a handful of prompts, but the real skill of setting a task up for a model, judging what comes back, and steering it through to something good.
This barely existed as a category three years ago.
But with no domain of their own, they can't tell when the AI is confidently wrong, and they compete with the model on exactly the ground where it's strongest.

kp.k: Diamond-complete competence combines depth, breadth and AI fluency
kp.d: The authors' diamond-complete ideal combines domain expertise, understanding of the whole workflow and skill in directing AI. They argue that only this combination compounds value with AI, and reiterate their earlier proposition that expertise and AI skill multiply rather than merely add. The diamond refers to an individual's competence, not a firm's staffing shape.
qs: Depth to know when the model is wrong. Breadth to see the whole workflow it sits inside. Fluency to direct it.
We've started calling the people who have all three at full length diamond-complete.
In our view, only this shape compounds in an age of AI.
expertise and AI skill multiply rather than add, so if either is missing you get very little.

kp.k: Expertise shifts toward directing and verifying AI
kp.d: The authors redefine depth away from outperforming a model unaided toward eliciting better-than-default outputs and catching domain-specific failures before harm occurs. They argue that improving AI increases the importance of expert verification because remaining errors become subtler, distinguishing an easily detected hallucinated citation from a plausible but incorrect claim.
qs: I know how to direct AI to get better results than it produces by default
I know where the model fails in my corner, and I catch it before it costs anything.
Domain expertise matters more as AI improves, because the better the model gets, the subtler and harder to spot its mistakes become.
A hallucinated citation is easy to catch; a plausible but quietly wrong claim is not.

kp.k: Automating junior work threatens the formation of judgment
kp.d: The authors warn that automating document review, first-pass models and other junior analyst tasks can eliminate the apprenticeship through which future senior judgment develops. They identify a tension between growing demand for sophisticated error detection and loss of the work that teaches it. Their own experience concerns established experts acquiring AI skills; they explicitly acknowledge uncertainty about how AI-skilled novices can acquire deep expertise.
qs: The judgment you need to catch the error rises at exactly the moment the work that built that judgment is being automated away.
We are much less clear on the reverse: how someone with AI skills but no anchor goes about building deep domain expertise from scratch, particularly in an AI-enabled world.
That junior work was never only cheap labour.
It was the apprenticeship: the years of doing the work badly, getting corrected, and slowly building the depth no one can shortcut.
Automate it away and you don't just save money; you remove the production line for the very anchor the diamond depends on.

kp.k: Develop domain anchors and preserve supervised apprenticeship
kp.d: The authors recommend identifying a specific domain where one can improve and verify model outputs, progressing from AI-assisted writing to directing and checking AI execution of a plan, and deliberately retaining junior participation in real work. Their proposed training arrangement gives juniors drafting responsibility, AI a critique role and seniors final judgment, preserving human supervision rather than relying directly on unchecked output.
qs: Name the specific corner where you can direct the model to create superior outputs and catch it when it's wrong.
Move from letting AI help you write toward creating a plan and having it execute while you direct and check.
If you lead people, don't let AI quietly eat the apprenticeship.
Put juniors, seniors, and AI on the same real problem — junior drafts, AI critiques, senior judges.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts and Brake argue that AI revalues expertise across knowledge work: narrow specialists and shallow generalists face substitution, while combining domain depth, breadth and AI-direction skills enables value to compound.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain argument, not a study of legal services specifically. The authors predict that advancing AI will progressively encroach on specialists' work, automating routine tasks before edge-case judgment. They argue that AI makes generalists' cross-domain synthesis abundant and inexpensive, turning apparent augmentation into substitution. Adding AI skills alone does not remedy a specialist's narrowness or a generalist's lack of domain grounding. Their proposed 'diamond-complete' professional combines depth, breadth and the ability to direct, evaluate and correct AI; this is a competence ideal, not a firm staffing structure. They redefine valuable depth as the ability to improve on AI's default outputs and catch domain-specific errors. They also claim that improving models make expertise more important because errors become subtler, while automation of junior work threatens the apprenticeship that develops such expertise.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers a conceptual framework, illustrative occupations and the authors' own experience, rather than quantified empirical evidence.
pts.d: Roberts and Brake ground the transition from domain expertise to AI fluency partly in their personal experience. They refer to their earlier writing for the proposition that expertise and AI skill multiply rather than add, but present no supporting data or study results here. Specialists such as radiologists, tax lawyers and credit analysts illustrate the framework; they are not empirical cases. The historical discussion of McKinsey and Tim Brown concerns the T-shaped expertise concept, not evidence for the AI displacement predictions. No benchmarks, measured productivity effects, employment statistics or legal-market findings are supplied. The authors explicitly acknowledge uncertainty about how AI-skilled newcomers can acquire domain depth.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2026 source describes revaluation as already underway and predicts continued capability advances, without specifying a deadline for displacement.
pts.d: The authors describe AI as having progressed over years from school-level competence toward professional judgment, with the frontier continuing to rise annually. They place the emergence of AI-direction skills within roughly the preceding three years. Specialist exposure is qualified by task type: routine work goes first and edge-case judgment lasts longest. Compounding value is conditional on combining domain depth, workflow breadth and substantive AI fluency, rather than merely knowing prompts. The apprenticeship warning is conditional on AI taking over work through which juniors previously learned. Their immediate recommendations are to identify a domain anchor, move toward AI execution under human direction and checking, and preserve junior participation in real work; these are proposals rather than demonstrated interventions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are knowledge-work specialists, generalists, multidisciplinary experts, AI-fluent newcomers, juniors and those responsible for their development.
pts.d: Narrow specialists, including tax lawyers, face erosion of previously protected tasks. Generalists face loss of the premium for connecting fields and synthesising information. AI-fluent generalists may help teams adopt technology but, according to the authors, lack the domain grounding needed to detect confidently wrong output. Professionals combining depth, breadth and AI fluency are positioned to direct work across whole workflows. Juniors risk losing opportunities to develop judgment, and employers risk weakening the future supply of senior expertise. The authors recommend shared junior–AI–senior work as a way to protect learning, retaining human judgment and checking rather than relying directly on unchecked AI outputs. The source makes no distinct claims about law-firm segments, legal-service pricing, ALSPs, in-house departments or access to justice.
